The study again, with the package

study-again.Rmd
library(decisions)

Overview

Can a decision model find defects in images of manufactured parts when it sees only a few reference images? And are its probabilities calibrated, so that a probability of 0.8 means that about 8 of 10 such parts are defective?

This vignette examines these questions with the package, on five datasets of industrial images. It repeats the steps of a study of decision models on these images (the original study; its record is public at https://fmegahed.github.io/decision-models-for-industrial-image-qc/). It tunes the descriptions of the answers, chooses the number of reference images and the image size, fits a calibrator, and saves each setup for one final test. It uses three models:

  • Jev, from TypeSafe, with decider_typesafe(). The version is pinned to jev-1.14.0, so a later version of Jev does not change the results.
  • gpt-6-luna, on the Decisions API of OpenAI, with decider_openai().
  • Clef-Flash, from Cloudflare, on a local SGLang server, with decider_systemone().

The results below come from live calls on 2026-10-23 and 2026-10-24. The package saved them in inst/extdata/study_again.rds, so this vignette builds without a key, a network or the images. The script data-raw/study_again.R in the source of the package made them. Its code is the code of this vignette.

Data

The five datasets come from a published study of image inspection with CLIP (Megahed et al., 2026). Each image is nominal (a good part) or defective.

Dataset Images Nominal Defective
extrusion Frames of the extrusion profile of a 3D printer normal over, under (too much or too little material)
microstructure Simulated microstructure images (EBSD) Uniform Band, Bimodal, SingleCrystal, each at a low, medium or high level
pan_images Surfaces of metallic pans nominal defective
pipe_staple A pipe staple on a car production line good missing (the staple is missing)
textiles Simulated textured surfaces nominal local (a small flaw), global (a change of the whole texture)

The authors of Megahed et al. (2026) recorded the extrusion images and simulated the microstructure images. The pan images come from Megahed and Camelio (2012). The authors simulated the textile images with the R package spc4sts (Bui & Apley, 2021). The pipe staple images come from the Automotive Visual Inspection Dataset (AutoVI) of Renault (Carvalho et al., 2024).

Licences

The images are in the public repository fmegahed/qe_genai, folder data/, under the MIT licence. The pipe staple images keep the licence of AutoVI, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0: give credit, use them for non-commercial work only, and share changed images under the same licence. The table study_sets.csv of the package holds only the image names and the labels. The package holds no image of these datasets, except the 50 textile images of vignette("images"). Here they are learning or reference images, not test images.

Images

Download the repository (about 360 MB):

git clone https://github.com/fmegahed/qe_genai.git

Then tell R where the images are, and where the state files, the setups and the test results go:

image_dir <- "qe_genai/data"
state_dir <- "state"
setup_dir <- "setups"
test_dir <- "test"
dir.create(state_dir)
dir.create(setup_dir)
dir.create(test_dir)

Rows

The table study_sets.csv gives each image one role. The image paths are relative to the folder data/ of fmegahed/qe_genai.

sets <- system.file("extdata", "study_sets.csv", package = "decisions") |>
  utils::read.csv() |>
  tibble::as_tibble() |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    truth = factor(
      dplyr::if_else(class == "nominal", "normal", "defective"),
      levels = c("normal", "defective")
    ),
    path = file.path(image_dir, image_path)
  )

by_dataset <- split(sets, sets$dataset)

table(sets$dataset, sets$role)
#>                 
#>                  calibration learning reference test
#>   extrusion               50       92         8  200
#>   microstructure          50       92         8  450
#>   pan_images               0       12         8   78
#>   pipe_staple             34       92         8  100
#>   textiles                50       92         8  200

The roles:

  • learning: labeled images to tune on. The tuning steps choose the descriptions and the image settings on these images.
  • reference: four images per class, with a rank from 1 to 4. A setup with k references per class uses the ranks 1 to k. The references come from the learning images. No step scores the references that its setup uses.
  • calibration: labeled images to fit the calibrator on. The pans have too few images for this role. For the pans, the calibrator uses the learning images and the references that the chosen setup does not use.
  • test: the images for the final estimate. They are scored one time only.

Each step of the tuning looks at the scores and keeps the better choice. A choice that looks better on the images that it was chosen on is, on average, less good on new images. So the estimate of a tuned setup on its own learning images is too high. The test images give an honest estimate only if no choice used them. So the test images are scored one time, at the end, after all choices are fixed. score_setup() refuses rows with the role test, and evaluate_once() scores them one time (see “Test”).

The original study drew the rows once, with fixed seeds.

Question

Each dataset gets the same choice question, with two answers. The instructions name inspection_image: that is the name of the input image in each request. The descriptions of the answers change during the tuning. The first candidate of each dataset is a generic description.

quality_question <- function(descriptions) {
  list(quality = question_choice(
    "Inspect `inspection_image` for manufacturing defects. Select exactly one category.",
    descriptions
  ))
}

generic <- c(
  normal = "No visible manufacturing defects; the part appears conforming.",
  defective = "At least one visible manufacturing defect or anomaly."
)

Models 

deciders <- list(
  jev = decider_typesafe("jev-1.14.0"),
  openai = decider_openai("gpt-6-luna"),
  clef = decider_systemone(
    "http://localhost:30000", "Cloudflare/clef-flash", image_format = "images"
  )
)

decider_typesafe() reads the key from the environment variable TYPESAFE_API_KEY, and decider_openai() from OPENAI_API_KEY (for example, in ~/.Renviron). Clef-Flash runs on your computer, on a GPU, and needs no key. The shell command below starts its server with Docker (vignette("images") has the details). It is not run here.

docker run --gpus all --shm-size 8g --ipc=host -p 30000:30000 \
  lmsysorg/sglang:dev-clef \
  sglang serve --model-path Cloudflare/clef-flash --host 0.0.0.0 --port 30000

The code below runs one model at a time. model_name is "jev", "openai" or "clef".

model_name <- "jev"

Setups

A setup holds one complete decision: the decider, the question with its descriptions, the reference images and the image settings. make_setup() makes the setup of one model and dataset with k references per class. upscale = TRUE enlarges each image to max_size pixels on its longest side: TypeSafe refuses images under 280 pixels, and some images of these datasets are smaller.

score_rows() scores a setup on labeled rows with score_setup(). It gives score_setup() the role of each row, so a test row stops the call before any request. A reference row counts as a learning row. Each run keeps its answers in a state file (path): a run that stops continues and does not pay twice. score_rows() also keeps the image paths with the result, so a later step can check that its rows are in the same order as the saved answers.

make_setup <- function(model, dataset, descriptions, k, max_size) {
  references <- by_dataset[[dataset]] |>
    dplyr::filter(role == "reference", rank <= k) |>
    dplyr::arrange(rank)
  decision_setup(
    deciders[[model]], quality_question(descriptions),
    references = list(
      normal = references$path[references$truth == "normal"],
      defective = references$path[references$truth == "defective"]
    ),
    max_size = max_size, upscale = TRUE
  )
}

score_rows <- function(setup, rows, path) {
  score_setup(
    setup, image = rows$path, truth = rows$truth,
    role = dplyr::if_else(rows$role == "reference", "learning", rows$role),
    path = path
  ) |>
    dplyr::mutate(image_path = list(rows$image_path))
}

state_file <- function(...) {
  file.path(state_dir, paste0(paste(..., sep = "_"), ".json"))
}

Wording

Candidates

The candidate descriptions come from description loops. In each loop, an agent (Claude Code) looked at 96 labeled images of one dataset (the learning images and the references of rank 3 and 4), in a sandbox folder that it could not leave. The image names gave no label. It wrote one candidate at a time: a new text for normal and for defective, from the images that the best candidate so far scored badly. A script scored each candidate, with two references per class, and gave the agent the ROC AUC. A loop had at most 6 candidates, and candidate 1 was the generic description.

The loops for Jev and Clef-Flash ran in the original study. gpt-6-luna got its own loops, with the same rules, scored with score_setup() of this package. The pans have no loop: they keep the generic description. The page description loops of the study record shows each candidate of the study loops with the reason for the change.

The saved results hold the candidates of all loops:

saved <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "study_again.rds", package = "decisions"))
candidates <- dplyr::select(
  saved$wording, model, dataset, candidate, normal, defective, reason
)

Keep rule

Two wordings can get a different AUC by chance alone: 96 images give a rough AUC. If each higher AUC replaced the best wording, the loop would follow this noise, and it would keep the wording that fits these 96 images by luck. The keep rule protects against this. A candidate replaces the current best only if its AUC is at least 0.02 higher. Candidate 1 is the first best.

keep_rule <- function(auc, gain = 0.02) {
  best <- purrr::accumulate(auc, \(best, x) {
    if (round(x - best, 10) >= gain) x else best
  })
  c(TRUE, diff(best) > 0)
}

round() removes the small errors of floating-point numbers, so a gain of exactly 0.02 counts.

Scores

The wording step scores the candidates of each loop in their order, on the same 96 images, with two references per class and max_size = 768. For Jev and Clef-Flash, these are new calls with the package. For gpt-6-luna, its loop already scored its candidates in this way, so its AUCs come from its loop logs, with no new call.

score_candidate <- function(model, dataset, candidate, normal, defective) {
  setup <- make_setup(
    model, dataset, c(normal = normal, defective = defective),
    k = 2, max_size = 768
  )
  design <- dplyr::filter(
    by_dataset[[dataset]],
    role == "learning" | (role == "reference" & rank > 2)
  )
  score_rows(setup, design, state_file("wording", model, dataset, candidate))
}

wording <- dplyr::filter(candidates, model == model_name)
wording <- wording |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    result = purrr::pmap(
      list(model, dataset, candidate, normal, defective), score_candidate
    ),
    auc = purrr::map_dbl(result, "estimate")
  )

The keep rule then gives the final wording of each dataset. The pans get the generic description.

wording <- dplyr::mutate(wording, kept = keep_rule(auc), .by = dataset)

final_wording <- wording |>
  dplyr::filter(kept) |>
  dplyr::slice_tail(n = 1, by = dataset) |>
  dplyr::select(model, dataset, normal, defective) |>
  dplyr::bind_rows(tibble::tibble(
    model = model_name, dataset = "pan_images",
    normal = generic[["normal"]], defective = generic[["defective"]]
  ))

The table gives, for each model and dataset, the number of candidates, the AUC of the generic description (candidate 1), the final candidate and its AUC.

model dataset candidates generic_auc final final_auc
jev extrusion 6 0.666 2 0.695
jev microstructure 4 0.804 2 0.918
jev pipe_staple 1 0.934 1 0.934
jev textiles 2 0.674 2 0.996
openai extrusion 6 0.613 5 0.770
openai microstructure 5 0.931 1 0.931
openai pipe_staple 2 0.828 2 0.999
openai textiles 6 0.743 5 0.966
clef extrusion 6 0.797 2 0.820
clef microstructure 5 0.901 4 0.953
clef pipe_staple 2 0.661 2 1.000
clef textiles 5 0.780 2 0.959

The loops raised the AUC of the generic description on most datasets. The largest gains: Clef-Flash on the pipe staples (0.66 to 1.00), Jev on the textiles (0.67 to 1.00), and gpt-6-luna on the textiles (0.74 to 0.97). For Jev on the pipe staples, the study loop stopped after the generic description. For gpt-6-luna on the microstructures, no candidate beat the generic description (0.93).

The keep rule worked as intended. For Clef-Flash on the textiles, candidate 2 scored 0.959 and candidate 4 scored 0.977. The gain of 0.018 is less than 0.02, so candidate 2 stayed the final wording.

These AUCs are on the images that the loops chose on, so they are too high (see “Rows”). The calibration and test images give fresher estimates.

The final descriptions of the textiles. Each model has its own loop, so each model has its own wording:

model normal defective
jev Grey fabric with a soft, smooth texture of long diagonal streaks that blend gently into each other; no spots, marks or areas that differ from the rest. Grey fabric with a visible anomaly: either a small local spot or mark, or a texture that is grainier, more speckled and noisier across the whole image, with short choppy strokes instead of long smooth diagonal streaks.
openai Gray fabric with a smooth, soft texture of long diagonal streaks running from lower left to upper right; clear darker and lighter bands and patches stand out, and the pattern looks the same across the whole image. Gray fabric where the texture is changed: either the whole image is covered by a fine, even, static-like grain with weak contrast, so the long diagonal streaks and dark bands are faint or washed out, or a tiny, sharp cluster of black and white pixels (often near an edge or corner) breaks the soft streak pattern.
clef Gray fabric with a uniform texture of smooth, soft diagonal streaks running evenly across the whole image; no spots or marks. Gray fabric where the texture differs from smooth even diagonal streaks: the whole surface looks rougher, coarser, mottled or clumpy, or there is a small spot, speck or foreign mark.

Grid

The grid tries 6 setups for each model and dataset: k = 1, 2 or 4 references per class, and max_size = 512 or 768 pixels. Each setup uses the final wording. It scores the learning images that are not references: 92 per dataset, and 12 for the pans. The setup with the highest AUC is the chosen setup. A tie goes to the smaller k, then to the smaller size.

score_grid <- function(model, dataset, normal, defective, k, max_size) {
  setup <- make_setup(
    model, dataset, c(normal = normal, defective = defective), k, max_size
  )
  learning <- dplyr::filter(by_dataset[[dataset]], role == "learning")
  score_rows(setup, learning, state_file("grid", model, dataset, k, max_size))
}

grid <- final_wording |>
  dplyr::cross_join(tibble::tibble(
    k = rep(c(1, 2, 4), each = 2), max_size = rep(c(512, 768), times = 3)
  ))
grid <- grid |>
  dplyr::mutate(result = purrr::pmap(
    list(model, dataset, normal, defective, k, max_size), score_grid
  ))
grid <- dplyr::bind_cols(
  dplyr::select(grid, -result),
  purrr::list_rbind(grid$result) |>
    dplyr::select(-metric) |>
    dplyr::rename(auc = estimate)
)

chosen <- grid |>
  dplyr::arrange(dataset, dplyr::desc(round(auc, 10)), k, max_size) |>
  dplyr::slice_head(n = 1, by = dataset)

No setting is the best for all models and datasets. On the extrusion images, the chosen setups use k = 1 (Jev), 4 (gpt-6-luna) and 4 (Clef-Flash). On the microstructures, they use k = 4, 1 and 1. Images of 512 pixels need about 49 % of the input tokens of images of 768 pixels, and they were often as good. 22 of the 90 setups reach an AUC of 1, all on the pans and pipe staples. The tie rule then picks the setup with the fewest references. On the 12 learning images of the pans, an AUC of 1 says little.

These AUCs are on the images that the grid chose on, so they are too high (see “Rows”). The calibration and test images give fresher estimates.

Calibration

A calibrator corrects the probabilities of a model, so that they agree with the rates of defects. This vignette uses Platt scaling: a logistic regression of the truth on the logit of the probability of defective. It is fitted on the calibration images, with the chosen setup.

calibration_rows <- function(dataset, k) {
  rows <- by_dataset[[dataset]]
  if (dataset == "pan_images") {
    dplyr::filter(rows, role == "learning" | (role == "reference" & rank > k))
  } else {
    dplyr::filter(rows, role == "calibration")
  }
}

score_calibration <- function(model, dataset, normal, defective, k, max_size) {
  setup <- make_setup(
    model, dataset, c(normal = normal, defective = defective), k, max_size
  )
  rows <- calibration_rows(dataset, k)
  score_rows(setup, rows, state_file("calibration", model, dataset, k, max_size))
}

calibration <- dplyr::select(chosen, model, dataset, normal, defective, k, max_size)
calibration <- calibration |>
  dplyr::mutate(result = purrr::pmap(
    list(model, dataset, normal, defective, k, max_size), score_calibration
  ))

Platt scaling does not fit the labels 0 and 1. With N+ defective and N- normal calibration images, its target is (N+ + 1) / (N+ + 2) for a defective image and 1 / (N- + 2) for a normal image. These targets keep the fit finite when a model ranks the few calibration images almost perfectly. A fit on the labels 0 and 1 then has no finite solution: its slope grows without limit, and the calibrated probabilities become 0 or 1. The logistic calibrator of probably (probably::cal_estimate_logistic() with smooth = FALSE) fits the labels 0 and 1, so it saturates on so few, almost perfectly ranked calibration images. On the calibration images of this vignette, its glm() warns for 8 of the 15 setups, and its calibrated probabilities come within 1e-12 of 0 or 1 for 9 setups. The calibrators of probably fit well with more calibration images. The targets are not 0 or 1, so the fit uses family = quasibinomial. clip() keeps each probability between 0.005 and 0.995, the clamp of the original study, so that its logit stays between about -5.3 and 5.3.

clip <- function(prob) pmin(pmax(prob, 0.005), 0.995)

platt_fit <- function(prob, truth) {
  n_defective <- sum(truth == "defective")
  n_normal <- sum(truth == "normal")
  target <- dplyr::if_else(
    truth == "defective", (n_defective + 1) / (n_defective + 2), 1 / (n_normal + 2)
  )
  stats::glm(target ~ stats::qlogis(clip(prob)), family = stats::quasibinomial())
}

platt_apply <- function(prob, intercept, slope) {
  stats::plogis(intercept + slope * stats::qlogis(clip(prob)))
}

platt_row() fits the Platt scaling of one setup and keeps its two coefficients and the class counts.

platt_row <- function(model, dataset, k, result, ...) {
  truth <- calibration_rows(dataset, k)$truth
  fit <- platt_fit(result$answers[[1]]$.pred_defective, truth)
  tibble::tibble(
    model = model, dataset = dataset,
    n_normal = sum(truth == "normal"), n_defective = sum(truth == "defective"),
    intercept = stats::coef(fit)[[1]], slope = stats::coef(fit)[[2]]
  )
}

platt <- calibration |>
  purrr::pmap(platt_row) |>
  purrr::list_rbind()

The setups keep no calibrator. write_setup() saves each setup as one JSON file, and the Platt fits stay in the saved results. So evaluate_once() scores the raw probabilities, and platt_apply() maps them to calibrated ones. (A setup can hold a probably calibrator when there are enough calibration images for it. Set it with setup@calibrator <- calibrator; this works also for a setup from read_setup().)

calibration |>
  dplyr::select(model, dataset, normal, defective, k, max_size) |>
  purrr::pwalk(\(model, dataset, normal, defective, k, max_size) {
    setup <- make_setup(
      model, dataset, c(normal = normal, defective = defective), k, max_size
    )
    write_setup(setup, file.path(setup_dir, paste0(model, "_", dataset, ".json")))
  })

All 15 fits converged, and glm() gave no warning. No fitted value reaches 0 or 1: the fitted values lie between 3.1e-04 and 1 - 2.3e-06. No fitted value lies within 1e-6 of 0 or 1. The clamp limits the logit, so it also limits the calibrated probability of any raw probability. But a steep fit multiplies the logit by its slope (up to 6.9, for Clef-Flash on the textiles). So at the clamp limits, 2 fits (Clef-Flash on the pipe staples and Clef-Flash on the textiles) give a calibrated probability within 1e-12 of 0 or 1.

The calibrated metrics:

calibration_metrics <- function(model, dataset, k, result, intercept, slope,
                                ...) {
  answers <- dplyr::mutate(
    result$answers[[1]], truth = calibration_rows(dataset, k)$truth
  )
  calibrated <- dplyr::mutate(
    answers, .pred_defective = platt_apply(.pred_defective, intercept, slope)
  )
  metrics <- yardstick::metric_set(
    yardstick::roc_auc, yardstick::brier_class, yardstick::mn_log_loss
  )
  dplyr::bind_rows(
    before = metrics(answers, truth, .pred_defective, event_level = "second"),
    after = metrics(calibrated, truth, .pred_defective, event_level = "second"),
    .id = "probabilities"
  ) |>
    dplyr::mutate(model = model, dataset = dataset, n = nrow(answers), .before = 1)
}

calibration_summary <- calibration |>
  dplyr::left_join(platt, by = c("model", "dataset")) |>
  purrr::pmap(calibration_metrics) |>
  purrr::list_rbind()

The table gives the AUC of the chosen setup on the calibration images, and the Brier score and the log loss before and after Platt scaling. A lower Brier score and a lower log loss are better. Platt scaling is strictly increasing between the clamp limits (its slope is positive in all 15 fits), so it keeps the order of the images there. Raw probabilities below 0.005, or above 0.995, become equal. On the calibration images, the AUC after Platt scaling is the same as before for all 15 setups. The AUC of the test comes from the raw probabilities.

Platt scaling is fitted and measured on the same images, so the numbers “after” are too good. The test images give the honest numbers.

The calibration images are new to the chosen setup (not for the pans: their calibration rows include the grid images), so their AUC is a first check of the choices. On most datasets, the AUC stays close to the AUC of the grid. On the extrusion images, the AUC of Jev falls from 0.77 (grid) to 0.61. This agrees with the effect that “Rows” describes: the choices fit the learning images better than new images. Chance plays a part too, because 50 images give a rough AUC.

Before calibration, the probabilities of the models are often too extreme. For gpt-6-luna on the extrusion images, the log loss is 3.84: the model gave probabilities near 0 or 1 to images of the other class. Platt scaling moves such probabilities toward the rates of defects, and the log loss falls to 0.57.

For Jev on the pans, Jev on the pipe staples, gpt-6-luna on the pans, Clef-Flash on the pans, and Clef-Flash on the pipe staples, the chosen setup separates the two classes of the calibration images fully (AUC 1). Their Platt fits stay finite, so their Brier score and log loss “after” stay above 0. The targets of Platt pull the probabilities a little away from 0 and 1. Where the raw probabilities are already good, this can make the numbers “after” worse: the Brier score or the log loss goes up for Jev on the pans and gpt-6-luna on the pans.

Folds

How much does an AUC move from one sample of images to another? Cross-validation splits the learning images of the chosen setup into 5 folds, 10 times (rsample::vfold_cv(), with the classes in the same ratio in each fold). Each fold gives the AUC of its fifth of the images. No model is fitted, and no call is sent: the folds use the saved probabilities of the grid.

fold_auc <- function(model, dataset, answers) {
  learning <- dplyr::filter(by_dataset[[dataset]], role == "learning")
  scored <- dplyr::mutate(answers, truth = learning$truth)
  set.seed(2026)
  rsample::vfold_cv(scored, v = 5, repeats = 10, strata = truth) |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      model = model, dataset = dataset,
      auc = purrr::map_dbl(splits, \(split) {
        held_out <- rsample::assessment(split)
        yardstick::roc_auc_vec(
          held_out$truth, held_out$.pred_defective, event_level = "second"
        )
      })
    ) |>
    dplyr::select(model, dataset, id, id2, auc)
}

folds <- chosen |>
  dplyr::select(model, dataset, answers) |>
  purrr::pmap(fold_auc) |>
  purrr::list_rbind()

The mean of the fold AUCs is close to the AUC of the grid, as it should be: the folds split the same images. The spread is the useful part. On the extrusion images, the AUC of about 18 images has a standard deviation of about 0.09, and it goes from 0.54 to 1.00 over the three models. On the microstructures and the textiles, the standard deviation is 0.05 or less. The standard deviation of an AUC falls about as 1 / sqrt(n). So for the 92 learning images of the extrusion, it is about 0.09 / sqrt(5), that is about 0.04: a difference of a few hundredths between two setups can come from chance. The pans give an AUC of 1 in 100 % of the folds, and the pipe staples in 97 %, so their folds show almost no spread.

Test

The test images give the final estimate of each chosen setup. No step above used them: the descriptions, the image settings and the Platt fits were fixed before the test. Before the run, the script data-raw/study_again.R checks that no learning, reference or calibration image has the path or the bytes (md5) of a test image. This check also shows that two extrusion test images are the same file, byte for byte; both stay in the test set. The numbers below come from one run on the test images, on 2026-10-24.

evaluate_once() reads the saved setup, which holds no calibrator, and scores the test images one time. So its AUC is the AUC of the raw probabilities. It writes the result to path and refuses to run again while that file exists. score_test() reads the result file when it exists, so a second run of this code sends no request and gives the same numbers.

test_file <- function(model, dataset) {
  file.path(test_dir, paste0(model, "_", dataset, ".rds"))
}

score_test <- function(model, dataset) {
  path <- test_file(model, dataset)
  if (file.exists(path)) {
    # The test rows were scored: read the result. No request goes out.
    return(dplyr::mutate(readRDS(path), calls = 0))
  }
  setup <- read_setup(file.path(setup_dir, paste0(model, "_", dataset, ".json")))
  test <- dplyr::filter(by_dataset[[dataset]], role == "test")
  evaluate_once(
    setup, image = test$path, truth = test$truth, event = "defective",
    path = path
  )
}
test <- chosen |>
  dplyr::select(model, dataset) |>
  dplyr::mutate(result = purrr::map2(model, dataset, score_test))

The Platt fit of each setup then gives the calibrated probabilities of the test images. test_metrics() computes with yardstick the AUC, the accuracy, the sensitivity (the share of defective images that the setup finds) and the specificity (the share of normal images that it passes) at a probability of 0.5, the Brier score and the log loss. It computes them before Platt scaling (raw) and after it (calibrated).

at_half <- function(prob) {
  factor(
    dplyr::if_else(prob >= 0.5, "defective", "normal"),
    levels = c("normal", "defective")
  )
}

test_metrics <- function(model, dataset, result, intercept, slope, ...) {
  truth <- dplyr::filter(by_dataset[[dataset]], role == "test")$truth
  metrics <- yardstick::metric_set(
    yardstick::roc_auc, yardstick::accuracy, yardstick::sensitivity,
    yardstick::specificity, yardstick::brier_class, yardstick::mn_log_loss
  )
  score <- function(prob) {
    scored <- tibble::tibble(truth = truth, prob = prob, predicted = at_half(prob))
    metrics(scored, truth, prob, estimate = predicted, event_level = "second")
  }
  raw <- result$answers[[1]]$.pred_defective
  dplyr::bind_rows(
    raw = score(raw),
    calibrated = score(platt_apply(raw, intercept, slope)),
    .id = "probabilities"
  ) |>
    dplyr::mutate(model = model, dataset = dataset, n = length(truth), .before = 1)
}

test_summary <- test |>
  dplyr::left_join(platt, by = c("model", "dataset")) |>
  purrr::pmap(test_metrics) |>
  purrr::list_rbind()

The AUC measures the ranking: it is the chance that a defective image gets a higher probability than a normal image. On the pans and the pipe staples, the AUC of each model is 0.995 or more. On the microstructures and the textiles, it lies between 0.934 and 1.000. The extrusion images are the hardest for all three models: their AUC lies between 0.733 and 0.842.

A good ranking does not give good decisions at a probability of 0.5. The raw probabilities of a model can fall mostly on one side of 0.5. For example, on the extrusion images, Clef-Flash gives no test image a raw probability of 0.5 or more (the highest is 0.495), although its AUC there is 0.842. So with the raw probabilities it calls every image normal, and its accuracy is 0.500. After Platt scaling, its accuracy is 0.745.

Platt scaling moves the probabilities toward the rates of defects of the calibration images. On most setups, this helps. The accuracy at 0.5 is higher after Platt scaling for 12 of the 15 setups, and the same for gpt-6-luna on the pipe staples. The Brier score and the log loss are both lower for 13 setups.

Platt scaling hurts Jev on the pans and gpt-6-luna on the pans. Their accuracy falls (Jev 0.987 to 0.885 and gpt-6-luna 0.808 to 0.654), their Brier score rises (Jev 0.053 to 0.075 and gpt-6-luna 0.118 to 0.163), and their log loss rises (Jev 0.236 to 0.287 and gpt-6-luna 0.356 to 0.465). The Platt fits of the pans come from only 18 images, and the grid chose the setup on most of these images (see “Calibration”), so these fits are rough.

The test sets are small. For the 78 pan images, one image on the wrong side changes the accuracy by 1.3 percentage points, and for the 100 pipe staple images by 1.0 points.

Cost and time of the test

Each test run sends one request per distinct image. The two extrusion test images that are the same file share one request (decide() sends identical inputs once), so images is 1,027 per model, for 1,028 test images. seconds is the sum of the response times, and minutes is the time of the whole run (10 requests at a time).

model images input_tokens cost seconds log_rows minutes
jev 1,027 7,437,499 NA 1,022.282 1,027 2.2
openai 1,027 2,606,155 NA 866.213 1,027 2.1
clef 1,027 1,706,215 NA 2,066.687 NA 4.0

log_rows is the number of paid calls that the script data-raw/study_again.R logged, one row per call. Clef-Flash runs on this computer and costs nothing per call, so it has no log. Each model scored its test images in 2.1 to 4.0 minutes.

The wording images of gpt-6-luna are the calls of its loops. No tuning step scored a test image.

Jev used about 2.6 times the input tokens of the other two models for the same images. The two hosted models answered in about 0.9 (Jev) and 1.1 (gpt-6-luna) seconds per image. Clef-Flash ran on one GPU (NVIDIA RTX 5000 Ada, 32 GB), and it took about 3.3 seconds per image, but it costs nothing per call. Once, during the wording step, the Clef-Flash server stopped answering. A restart of the server and a new run with the same state files continued the step: the finished answers came from the state files, and only the open images were sent again.

Image size

The setup here differs slightly from the paper of the original study. This vignette enlarges each image to 512 or 768 pixels on its longest side (upscale = TRUE; the large pan images are made smaller). The paper used 1,568 pixels, with padding.
